summary: Specifies a combination of the secure RTP profile (SAVP) and the feedback profile (AVPF), allowing secure real-time communication with timely receiver feedback. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5124 defines SAVPF, an RTP profile that combines secure media transport with timely RTCP feedback. It lets a session use the security features of SAVP and the feedback features of AVPF together.

questions: can secure and insecure rtp profiles be mixed
how is savpf negotiated in sdp
subtitle: A secure RTP profile that combines SRTP protection with AVPF's timely receiver feedback.

tldr.problem: The secure RTP profile SAVP and the feedback profile AVPF are separate profiles, but real-time sessions may need both protection and timely receiver feedback.
tldr.mechanism: SAVPF combines SAVP's SRTP security layer with AVPF's feedback timing and packet formats, then defines how endpoints negotiate the combined profile.
tldr.outcome: A secure RTP session can use AVPF feedback. SAVPF inherits SAVP's security properties and introduces no additional security services.

today: RFC 5124 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2008. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Combining Security and Feedback
sections.content:
Secure RTP (SAVP) provides encryption, integrity protection, and replay protection. The RTP/AVPF profile lets session participants send timely feedback while maintaining the average RTCP data rate. Both are RTP profiles that must be negotiated, and a single RTP session could previously select one profile rather than both.

RFC 5124 defines SAVPF, a profile combining SAVP and AVPF. The RFC treats the profiles as largely independent and describes the implications of using them together and the negotiation rules.
sections.plainLanguage: SAVPF lets an RTP session use SRTP security and AVPF feedback at the same time. It combines two existing profiles rather than replacing their separate functions.

sections.title: How SAVPF Layers Its Functions
sections.content:
SAVP operates between RTP and the transport layer, usually UDP. In SAVPF, AVPF replaces AVP at the upper layer. AVPF controls RTCP timing and defines feedback packet formats; those rules work whether or not RTCP packets are encrypted or integrity-protected.

The SAVP behavior remains unchanged: SRTP adds security fields and applies cryptographic transforms. All RTCP packets MUST be encapsulated as defined in RFC 3711. AVPF feedback formats MAY be used. The RTCP encryption prefix from RFC 3550 MUST NOT be used in SAVPF.
sections.plainLanguage: AVPF determines when feedback is sent, and SRTP protects RTP and RTCP packets. SAVPF applies both sets of rules in one session.

sections.title: Security Overhead and Feedback Frequency
sections.content:
AVPF's feedback frequency depends on RTCP bandwidth, group size, and average RTCP packet size. SRTCP adds fields to each RTCP packet, probably at least 10 to 20 bytes, with 14 bytes as the default. Extensions or different field lengths may add more.

Larger RTCP packets can reduce how frequently feedback is sent. Application designers MUST account for the SRTCP packet size by adjusting the RTCP variable avg_rtcp_size, so bandwidth shares remain appropriate.
sections.plainLanguage: Security fields make RTCP packets larger. Because AVPF uses packet size when scheduling feedback, applications must include that extra size in their calculations.

sections.title: Negotiating SAVPF
sections.content:
SDP identifies the combined profile as RTP/SAVPF. Attributes defined for SAVP and AVPF MAY also be used with SAVPF. During offer/answer negotiation, AVP, AVPF, SAVP, and SAVPF are mutually exclusive choices for one media description, though different media sessions may use different profiles.

An offerer that supports multiple acceptable profiles SHOULD list them in preference order and prefer secure profiles. An offer SHOULD NOT combine secure and insecure alternatives unless the signaling is appropriately protected. If an offer requires SAVPF and the answerer does not support it, the media session MUST be rejected. With RTSP, the client selects one profile for each media stream in SETUP, and the server confirms or refuses it.

For announcements without interactive negotiation, the initiator SHOULD provide acceptable alternatives. AVP or AVPF SHOULD NOT be announced when security is desired unless other security measures are used.
sections.plainLanguage: Endpoints agree on one profile for each media session. If an offer requires SAVPF and the other endpoint does not support it, that media session is rejected.

sections.title: Which Profiles Can Share a Session
sections.content:
SAVP and SAVPF use SRTP, while AVP and AVPF use plain RTP unless another security mechanism is applied. Secure and insecure profiles MUST NOT be mixed within one RTP session.

SAVP and SAVPF entities MAY share an RTP session, following the interworking considerations in RFC 4585. AVP and AVPF entities MAY also share a session. Different RTP sessions may use different profiles.
sections.plainLanguage: Secure RTP and plain RTP cannot be mixed in one RTP session. SAVP and SAVPF can share a session, as can AVP and AVPF.

sections.title: Security and Key Limits
sections.content:
SAVPF inherits its security properties from SAVP and adds or removes no security services. Applying SAVPF implies integrity protection for RTCP, which prevents false packets from non-members but does not protect against a malicious group member.

Security SHOULD NOT be traded for interoperability. The RFC recommends avoiding insecure profile alternatives for confidential or integrity-protected groups unless other security mechanisms are in place. A master key MUST NOT be shared among different RTP sessions unless their SSRC values are unique across all streams using that key. When the key has secured 2^48 SRTP packets or 2^31 SRTCP packets, whichever comes first, key management MUST provide new keys or the session MUST end. IANA registers RTP/SAVPF as the SDP protocol value.
sections.plainLanguage: SAVPF provides the same security services as SAVP. Keys must be replaced or the session ended when either packet limit is reached, and insecure alternatives should not weaken a session's security.
